questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman was reviewed 36 hours after sustaining a monkey bite to her arm from a wild macaque in Zambia. She had cleaned the wound immediately with soap and water and applied an OTC antimicrobial ointment. She took oral azithromycin to prevent bacterial superinfection and had returned to the United States for urgent medical care. Prior to her travel, she had received immunization for hepatitis A; combined tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis; and typhoid. She was taking mefloquine for malaria prophylaxis. On physical examination, she was anxious. Temperature was 37°C, pulse rate 84 beats/minute, and blood pressure 135/84 mmHg. The left upper arm had multiple scratches and deep bite marks, which were minimally inflamed.
questions.lead_in: In addition to rabies immunization, what is the most appropriate additional postexposure prophylaxis?

options.text: Foscarnet, twice daily for one week
Valaciclovir 1 gram PO every 8 hours for 2 weeks

questions.explanation: Valaciclovir 1 gram PO every 8 hours for 2 weeks This question relates to the risk of herpes B virus infection. There is a small risk for transmission, but herpes B virus infection can cause fatal encephalomyelitis in humans after bites and scratches. In humans, herpes B virus prophylaxis is indicated to avoid disease, especially in a deep wound like this. Long courses of postexposure prophylaxis are recommended for high-risk exposures like the patient above. It is reasonable to consider an individual uninfected if symptomfree and seronegative at 12 weeks. Valaciclovir 1 gram PO every 8h for 2 weeks is the recommend prophylaxis. Alternative options include aciclovir and valganciclovir. There is no known advantage to using either cidofovir or foscarnet, both of which are more toxic than valaciclovir and must be given IV . Treatment of established disease: IV aciclovir or IV ganciclovir. Ribavirin is used as PEP for Lassa fever and CCHF but has no efficacy against herpes B virus.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q8

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman was bitten by a Rhesus macaque on the forearm. The wound was thoroughly irrigated after the injury, and she was started on amoxicillin/clavulanate.
questions.lead_in: What other prophylactic agent should she be offered?
questions.explanation: Aciclovir Monkey bites involving macaques carry the risk for transmission of B virus, a herpesvirus that can cause fatal encephalomyelitis in humans. Postexposure prophylaxis with either aciclovir or valaciclovir is appropriate.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q28

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman developed fever and worsening confusion that evolved over 1 week. A collateral history was obtained from her partner. She worked as a zookeeper. She was usually assigned to the alligators but 2 weeks prior to presentation, she had been asked to care for the macaques as well. She had been bitten by one of the pregnant macaques and sustained a minor wound in her hand. Six months previously, she had traveled to South Africa for wilderness training related to her work. During this training, she encountered a lot of wild animals including monkeys, giraffes, lions, hyenas, and vultures. She did not take malarial and typhoid prophylaxis before the trip and had sustained multiple tick and mosquito bites. On physical exam, she had a temperature of 40.1°C and blood pressure of 140/100 mmHg. She was disoriented and confused; there was no nuchal or muscle rigidity. Investigations: MRI brain: normal appearances CSF exam: pleocytosis (lymphocyte predominant), normal glucose, and elevated total protein
questions.lead_in: What strategy could have prevented her from developing encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Aciclovir prophylaxis Fever, confusion, and a cerebrospinal fluid exam that shows lymphocytic-predominant pleocytosis with normal glucose suggest viral encephalitis. A recent history of a bite from a macaque should raise the suspicion for herpes B virus (also called B virus) infection, which is essentially the homologue of herpes simplex virus infection in macaques. B virus causes human encephalitis that is indistinguishable from other causes of viral encephalitis. Aciclovir postexposure prophylaxis after a macaque bite is recommended to prevent B virus infection. Although the patient should have received appropriate advice on using antimosquito repellent and prophylaxis for malaria prior to her trip, malaria and tick-associated illnesses would have manifested earlier after her return from South Africa. Her clinical presentation is also not consistent with tetanus.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q16

questions.question: A patient in India is bitten by a macaque and given amoxicillin/clavulanate and a tetanus booster.
questions.question_raw: Q55 (2013 PM). Patient in India is bitten by a macaque and given Amox/Clav and Tetanus booster.

parts.text: What are two fatal infections they are at risk of?

parts_raw.text: A) What are 2 fatal infections they are at risk of?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Herpes B virus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1) encephalomyelitis (untreated mortality ~70-80%). (2) Rabies.
b) (1) Valacyclovir (1 g PO tid x14d) or acyclovir for herpes B virus postexposure prophylaxis. (2) Rabies immune globulin. (3) Rabies vaccine.
questions.beyond_mandell: Rabies risk and rabies PEP (RIG + vaccine) are not from this chapter; per WHO/CDC rabies postexposure prophylaxis for a macaque bite in a rabies-endemic region.

cohort_answer.text:
Herpes B virus; Rabies
Rabies Ig and vaccine; Acyclovir, B virus specific Ig if available

questions.question: For each pathogen, what is the animal reservoir?
questions.question_raw: For each virus, what is the animal reservoir?
questions.model_answer: a) Herpes B (Macacine herpesvirus 1): macaque monkeys (Old World macaques, e.g. rhesus and cynomolgus). b) Sin Nombre virus: the deer mouse, Peromyscus maniculatus. c) Rabies: mammalian reservoirs vary by region—in North America, bats plus terrestrial carnivores (raccoons, skunks, foxes); worldwide the dog is the dominant reservoir. d) Chlamydia psittaci: psittacine birds (parrots, parakeets, cockatiels) and other birds.

cohort_answer.text: Herpes B: Macaque monkey. Sin Nombre virus: Deer mouse/rat. Rabies: Bats and raccoons. Chlamydia psittaci: Parrots.

questions.question: A worker in a research lab is bitten by a macaque that has been kept in the lab for the last 3 years.
questions.question_raw: A worker in a research lab is bitten by a Macaque, which has been kept in the lab for the last 3 years – (2019)

parts.text: What makes this situation high risk?

parts_raw.text: What makes this situation high risk?

questions.model_answer:
a) Herpes B virus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1) infection, which ascends the peripheral nervous system to cause a fatal encephalomyelitis (untreated mortality ~70-80%).
b) A macaque bite penetrating the skin from an animal whose oral/genital/ocular secretions may be shedding virus; deep puncture bites are difficult to clean, and bites to the head/face let virus rapidly reach the CNS. Captive macaques are commonly seropositive.
c) Valacyclovir 1 g PO tid, or acyclovir 800 mg PO 5 times daily, for 14 days, begun within 5 days of exposure after thorough wound irrigation.

cohort_answer.text: Concern: B virus infection - fatal encephalomyelitis. High risk factors: Deep wound puncture bite with saliva secretions; virus shed from oral and genital secretions; 20-100% of captive macaques are seropositive; higher risk if wound involving head or neck. Prophylaxis: Valacyclovir 1g q8h x14d; consider rabies vaccination and immunoglobulin (although in lab for 3 yrs), tetanus vaccination and/or antibiotic prophylaxis

questions.question: A laboratory worker calls after being bitten by a macaque monkey that has been in the lab for 3 years.
questions.question_raw: A laboratory worker calls after being bit by a macaque monkey. The monkey has been in the lab for 3 years.

parts.text: What important zoonotic infection can be transmitted to humans from laboratory monkeys?
What aspect of this case makes this a high-risk exposure?
Which agent is needed for post-exposure prophylaxis?

parts_raw.text: a) What important zoonotic infection can be transmitted to humans from laboratory monkeys?
b) What aspect of this case makes this a high-risk exposure?
c) Which agent is needed for post-exposure prophylaxis?

questions.model_answer:
a) Herpes B virus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1), for which macaques are the natural reservoir; causes fatal encephalomyelitis in humans.
b) A bite (loss of skin integrity) from a macaque, which can shed virus in oral/genital/ocular secretions; deep puncture bites are hard to clean and virus can ascend to the CNS.
c) Valacyclovir 1 g PO tid (drug of choice) or acyclovir 800 mg PO 5 times daily for 14 days.

cohort_answer.text: Herpes Virus B (Herpesvirus simiae, only macaque family monkeys are natural reservoir). High risk: monkey bit the person; bites/scratches penetrating skin higher risk, wounds to head/neck/torso can rapidly spread to CNS. PEP: specific B virus immunoglobulin if available, prophylaxis with Valacyclovir 1g PO q8h x14 days or Acyclovir 800mg PO 5x daily x14 days.

questions.question: A lab worker is bitten by a macaque that has been in the lab for the past 3 years.
questions.question_raw: Lab worker bitten by macaque in lab for the past 3 years.

parts.text: Why is this considered a high risk exposure?

parts_raw.text: Why is this considered a high risk exposure?

questions.model_answer:
a) Herpes B virus (Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1) infection causing fatal encephalomyelitis.
b) A macaque bite penetrating skin from an animal that intermittently sheds virus in oral/genital/ocular secretions; deep puncture bites are difficult to clean and virus can travel to the CNS, and captive macaques are frequently seropositive.
c) Valacyclovir 1 g PO tid or acyclovir 800 mg PO 5 times daily for 14 days, started as early as possible and within 5 days of exposure, after thorough wound cleansing.

cohort_answer.text: Cercopithecine herpesvirus 1 (CeHV-1)/Simian herpes B virus - zoonotic agent causing fatal encephalomyelitis. High risk because: all captive macaques considered infected, virus persists in sensory ganglia with intermittent shedding, fatal encephalomyelitis in 70% if untreated; high risk exposures include skin exposure with loss of integrity, mucosal exposure, lacerations of head/neck/torso, deep puncture bite, needlestick with CNS tissue/fluid, exposure to lesion fluid known to contain virus, positive post-cleansing culture. Prophylaxis: Valacyclovir 1g PO TID x14d, initiated within 5 days of exposure
